name: Plasmacytoid dendritic cell
markers: CD11c (absent or very low on human cells; low on mouse cells)
TLR7 and TLR9 (inside the cell, in endosomes)
BST2 / PDCA-1 (mouse marker; many other cells make it after interferon)
summary: A rare cell named for its plasma-cell-like look. It senses viral genetic material through TLR7 and TLR9 and within hours releases huge amounts of type I interferon, which puts nearby cells on antiviral alert and helps activate NK cells. It lives in blood and in the T-cell areas of lymphoid organs. Whether it presents antigen well is debated.
functions: Senses viral nucleic acids inside endosomes: TLR7 detects single-stranded RNA and TLR9 detects unmethylated CpG DNA. Human plasmacytoid cells make these two receptors strongly, while monocytes use mainly other Toll-like receptors.

Makes very large amounts of type I interferon (IFN-α and IFN-β) within hours of sensing a virus, about 200 to 1000 times more than other white blood cells in human blood. The signal runs through the adaptor MyD88 and the transcription factor IRF-7, which mouse studies show is essential. Why these cells are so much better at this than any other cell is not fully explained.
Also makes type III interferon (IFN-λ) in a subset of human cells, together with TNF and IL-6.

Activates NK cells and supports virus-specific CD8 T cells through interferon. Shown mainly in mice: in cytomegalovirus infection, spleen plasmacytoid cells mature, make interferon and help activate NK cells, and in mice depleted of them the CD8 T-cell response to vesicular stomatitis virus survives less well.

In the spleen (mouse evidence): sits in the T-cell area, and within hours of a TLR7 or TLR9 signal clusters in the marginal zone and the outer T-cell area. Spleen plasmacytoid cells are a main source of interferon early in cytomegalovirus infection. Most of this work is in mice.

Leaves the blood for lymph nodes and for injured skin. It crosses the walls of high endothelial venules into lymph nodes, using L-selectin, the chemoattractant chemerin and, in mice, CCR7. In skin wounds (seen in mouse and human wounds) it senses DNA released from damaged cells and makes interferon that helps drive early inflammation and the closing of the wound.

After a viral signal, or IL-3 with CD40L in culture, it matures into a dendritic-cell-like cell that raises MHC class II and co-stimulators. In culture, human cells matured by virus push naive CD4 T cells to make IFN-γ and IL-10.
Helps B cells become antibody-secreting plasma cells: in human cells in culture, interferon from virus-stimulated plasmacytoid cells starts the change and IL-6 completes it.
Can push T cells towards regulation instead of attack: in human cells in culture, CpG-activated cells induce regulatory T cells, and cells with high ICOS-L induce IL-10-producing regulatory T cells.

Debated: how well it presents antigen. Older work showed that activated cells can prime T cells, but some of that activity may belong to look-alike cells inside the old plasmacytoid gate (the AS-DCs and pre-DCs seen in human blood in 2017). In mice only plasmacytoid cells of myeloid origin process and present antigen well, and in one mouse study they primed naive CD4 T cells in lymph nodes but not in the spleen.

Debated: where it comes from. It needs FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor E2-2 (TCF4), but mouse studies disagree on whether it arises from myeloid or lymphoid progenitors, and it may come from both.
abundance: Rare. Well under 1% of white blood cells in human blood. In mice they are a small subset of spleen cells, with frequencies that differ between mouse strains; they are found in blood, lymph nodes and spleen but are scarce in healthy tissues, and flow into skin wounds and inflamed tissue.
